body_text: Thus commenced the Battle for Aero Supremacy. Not another race passed where a new wrinkle wasn’t introduced. It wasn’t immediately clear whether this was a testament to the technical ingenuity of Formula 1 or to one-upmanship run amok. Wings moved farther forward and farther back. They grew wider and taller, then wider and taller still. They were attached to the bodywork. They were attached to the hubs. They were fixed. They were adjustable. The system operated by compressed air. Or by electrohydraulics. Or via cable or bungee cord. The drivers moved the wings as they saw fit, or the wings moved automatically, depending on whether the brakes were applied, or fifth gear was selected, or the moon was in the seventh house of the seventh sun and Jupiter was aligned with Mars. By the fall of 1968, every car sported wings varied enough to confound an ornithologist. [The Deadliest Decade chronicles pro racing from 1964 to 1973, when the influx of money and technology caused speeds to skyrocket while racetracks remained unchanged. The carnage that followed sparked outrage that transformed attitudes about safety and spawned the creation of the modern safety industry. This is the second of three excerpts, and you can read the first here . The book is available for preorder at Octane Press . — Ed. ] Jacky Ickx, cornering in a Brabham Cosworth BT26A at the 1969 Spanish Grand Prix, was in second place when his rear wing failed. After it was replaced, he returned to the race but retired with rear suspension failure, a result of the previous mechanical problem. David Phipps/Sutton Images/Getty Images Some outsiders wondered if it was all just a game of monkey see, monkey do, and skeptics suggested that the major benefit of wings was that they made the drivers feel more confident. The teams knew better. At Monza, a wingless BRM emerged from Curva Grande—the intimidating sweeper at the end of the pit straight—at 156 mph. With a wing, the exit speed was 168 mph. Tire temperature, meanwhile, climbed from 130 degrees to 160 degrees, which demonstrated how much more grip was being developed. Lap times were an even better barometer. Bruce McLaren reported early in the wing-development game that aero aids were worth one to one-and-a-half seconds a lap. By the final race of the season in Mexico City, the fastest lap, recorded by Jo Siffert in a high-wing Lotus 49, was nearly four seconds faster than Jim Clark had gone in an aerodynamically clean version of the same car the previous year. Wings were great, everybody agreed. Exactly why, nobody knew for sure. “We didn’t have any wind tunnels,” said Herbie Blash, a longtime FIA official who was then a mechanic at Lotus. “It was just, ‘Stick this on’ and ‘Stick that on.’ Colin [Chapman] was flying his own plane, so he obviously understood aerodynamics to a certain degree. But we had no real technical knowledge about what would work and what wouldn’t work.” And what empirical data existed was derived almost entirely from what happened when new untested parts were deployed on race weekends. Fast-and-dirty prototype development has a lot going for it, but it also means taking the bad with the good. In the case of wings, failure was an option, and it occurred early and often. By the time the teams reached Rouen for the French Grand Prix, Chapman had soured on the small, vestigial wing that debuted at Monaco. Now, in typical Chapman fashion, he’d fitted his Lotus 49Bs with the biggest, tallest, most outrageous wings in Formula 1. In the garage, young Jackie Oliver, who’d been hurriedly drafted into the team after Clark’s death, pushed on the airfoil, which made a disquieting boinggg! sound as it visibly vibrated on the slender mounting struts. “Is that all right?” he asked. To which Chapman scornfully replied, “Lad, when you sit on an airplane and you look out the window when it takes off, the wing is flexing because that’s what keeps it from breaking.” Oliver shelved his doubts, and when he headed out for practice, he was pleased to experience “fantastic” levels of grip—briefly. On his third flying lap, streaking past the grandstands at 190 mph, he closed on Richard Attwood’s BRM, which was just coming out of the pits. As Attwood moved over to allow Oliver to pass, the turbulent air behind him tilted back the wing of the Lotus so that it was generating lift instead of downforce. Uh-oh. The rear wheels levitated off the ground, and the car walloped a low wall so hard that the gearbox, transaxle, and rear wheels broke off as a single assembly, leaving Oliver dazed and confused in what was pretty much the only part of the chassis that hadn’t been destroyed. Skid marks and wreckage show how fortunate Jackie Oliver was to escape a practice run crash in a Lotus 49B, French Grand Prix, 1968. David Phipps/Sutton Images/Getty Images Chapman, who had a fractious relationship with most of his drivers unless they were named Clark or Andretti, blamed Oliver for losing control. Despite the accident, and even though several observers told Chapman that they’d seen the Lotus’s wings flexing conspicuously at speed, he opted for even higher airfoils at the next race, Brands Hatch. The wings survived the British Grand Prix; in fact, Oliver would have won if his transmission hadn’t disintegrated while he was leading. This time, John Surtees was the one with wing woes. After the freshly mounted airfoil on his Honda RA301 snapped off, he finished the race with the naked struts blowing in the wind and a set of bald rear tires, thanks to the sudden lack of grip. At the U.S. Grand Prix, the rear wing of Jochen Rindt’s Brabham BT26 collapsed at both ends so that it looked like a tepee built with an erector set. At the next race, in Mexico, a strut on local hero Moisés Solana’s Lotus 49B broke, forcing him to pit to have the wing ripped off and trashed. By the time the 1969 season began in South Africa, F1 was deep in the throes of wing mania. Lotus, Brabham, and Matra all showed up with biplane arrangements—two sets of high wings, front and rear. During practice, Kyalami looked more like an airport than a racetrack. The wings of two of the Lotuses and both of the Brabhams failed during practice or the race. Still, Jackie Stewart won in a biplane-equipped Matra MS10, outrunning Hill in his twin-wing Lotus. At Montjuïc Park, the twisty street circuit in Barcelona hosting the Spanish Grand Prix, Chapman reasoned that he needed even bigger wings. After practice on Friday, Lotus mechanics worked into the night fabricating 6-inch-wide extensions with fiberglass and foam to either side of the rear wing. “No testing, no scrutineering,” said mechanic Beaky Sims. “It shows what you could do back then.” Jochen Rindt, in a Lotus Cosworth 49B, was leading the race by a huge margin when he suffered a rear wing failure at over 160 mph at the Spanish Grand Prix, 1969. David Phipps/Sutton Images/Getty Images Despite the lack of testing, the Lotuses qualified 1-3 in the hands of Rindt and Hill. Rindt led from the flag and walked away from the field. As he started his ninth lap, Hill’s wing collapsed after he crested the bump on the front straight at 160 mph, and his car was demolished when it rammed into the guardrail on the left and ricocheted into the Armco on the right. Hill was unhurt. But as Sims ran out from the pits, Hill saw the wing sagging on Rindt’s car. “His wing is going! His wing is going!” he yelled. “Beaky, get back to the pits and tell Chapman to bring him in.” Too late. When Sims was halfway there, he heard a huge crash as Rindt’s wing failed. Rindt cannoned into Hill’s wrecked Lotus and then vaulted onto the guardrail. If the launch angle had been slightly higher, he would have landed in the crowd. As it was, Sims said, “The nose of the car was bent up like a banana. We couldn’t get [Rindt] out, and we could hear the battery shorting, and we could smell fuel. Finally, Graham got astride the car and just yanked him out.” *** The post The Deadliest Decade: The Battle for Aero Supremacy appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: Qu’est-ce que le PHPP dans la fabrication ?
summary: Comprendre le rôle du PPAP dans l'assurance qualité de la fabrication
body_text: Les normes de qualité garantissent que les pièces et les produits des clients fonctionnent comme prévu, soient sûrs et conformes à la réglementation. Notre processus de production standard comprend l’analyse de la conception pour la fabrication (DFM), qui est la première étape pour garantir la qualité d’une pièce moulée. En outre, nous mesurons jusqu’à quatre dimensions de plan à plan et de diamètre extérieur à partir de votre modèle CAO (X, Y et Z) par rapport aux tolérances indiquées. Notre entreprise est également certifiée ISO 9001:2015 et enregistrée ITAR. Protolabs produit des pièces rapidement et de manière constante en combinant la fabrication numérique et les procédés de moulage scientifiques, ainsi que des méthodes d’assurance et de contrôle de la qualité. Le processus d’homologation des pièces de production (PHPP) est un rapport d’inspection populaire pour les pièces moulées et l’un des contrôles de qualité les plus importants pour les industries aux normes élevées. En quoi consiste le processus d’homologation des pièces de production ? Les mesures de contrôle de la qualité sont essentielles dans le secteur de la fabrication, quelle que soit l'industrie. Les normes de qualité garantissent que les pièces et les produits des clients fonctionnent comme prévu, soient sûrs et conformes à la réglementation. Protolabs produit des pièces rapidement et de manière constante en combinant la fabrication numérique et les procédés de moulage scientifiques, ainsi que des méthodes d’assurance et de contrôle de la qualité. Notre processus de production standard inclut l’analyse de la conception pour la fabrication (DFM), qui constitue la première étape pour garantir la qualité d’une pièce moulée. En outre, nous mesurons jusqu’à quatre dimensions de plan à plan et de diamètre extérieur à partir de votre modèle CAO (X, Y et Z) par rapport aux tolérances indiquées. Notre entreprise est également certifiée ISO 9001:2015 et enregistrée ITAR. En plus de notre processus standard, nous proposons diverses options de mesure de la qualité, d’inspection et de documentation, en collaborant avec vous pour nous assurer que nous respectons notre norme stricte de livraison de pièces moulées par injection de haute qualité. Les options de rapport d’inspection comprennent des méthodes de mesure telles que le processus d’homologation des pièces de production (PHPP), divers points de contrôle du premier article, l’inspection critique pour la qualité et les rapports d’inspection numériques, qui sont disponibles lors de la commande. Cet article de blog est axé sur le premier, le PHPP pour les pièces moulées. Comme toujours, vous pouvez consulter l’un de nos experts en moulage par injection pour déterminer les options d’inspection les plus appropriées par rapport aux exigences de votre projet. En quoi consiste le processus d’homologation des pièces de production ? Le PHPP est né dans l’industrie automobile, où les ingénieurs ont créé une procédure précise et normalisée pour s’assurer que le processus de fabrication ou les capacités d’un fournisseur produisent systématiquement des pièces conformes aux spécifications du client. Notre offre standard PHPP est similaire à un PHPP de niveau 3 traditionnel. Nous le faisons en utilisant les informations que vous fournissez. Le formulaire contient des informations de base sur la pièce et le processus utilisés au moment du devis et de la commande. Le PHPP comprend les résultats des options d’inspection sélectionnées par le client, qui identifient les exigences dimensionnelles de votre pièce. Consultez cet exemple de notre solution PHPP. Le pack PHPP comprend plusieurs des 19 éléments traditionnels qui démontrent la répétabilité et la fiabilité des processus utilisés pour fabriquer votre pièce. Les organigrammes de processus, l’AMDEC, les plans de contrôle, les plans d’inspection, les résultats dimensionnels, les certificats de conformité et les garanties de soumission des pièces sont tous des éléments standard du PHPP. Nous conservons des enregistrements de lots pour les pièces de production d’échantillons et les échantillons maîtres à côté de votre moule. Chaque devis comprend une analyse spécifique de la pièce avec le DFM et les risques associés. Notre PHPP standard a un impact minimal sur les délais de livraison indiqués dans votre devis. Si vous avez des exigences supplémentaires, la sélection d’un PHPP personnalisé via notre sélecteur de services supplémentaires déclenchera un processus d’examen par notre équipe, ce qui nous permettra de faire appel à un prestataire d’inspection certifié externe. Notre équipe vous aidera à déterminer vos besoins spécifiques. Les PHPP personnalisés nécessitent un délai supplémentaire. Ce délai supplémentaire sera indiqué au moment de la commande de la pièce et est généralement compris entre 3 et 5 jours ouvrables, selon le niveau de PHPP. Utilisation du PHPP dans l’industrie La plupart des industries utilisent désormais le PHPP comme option, parallèlement à d’autres méthodes d’inspection de la qualité. Les entreprises des secteurs de l’automobile, de l’aérospatiale, du médical, de l’électronique grand public, des équipements industriels lourds et d’autres secteurs utilisent le PHPP. L ’industrie automobile , qui a été la première à utiliser le PHPP, l’exige en fait, car le processus est normalisé dans toute la fabrication automobile. L’ industrie aérospatiale , avec ses nombreux facteurs à haut risque que l’on retrouve dans un large éventail d’applications commerciales, industrielles et militaires/de défense, l’exige à la fois pour le développement de nouveaux produits et pour les modifications de produits existants dans les segments de l’aérospatiale et de la défense. Dans le secteur médical, le PHPP est exigé lors de l’introduction d’un nouveau produit ou de la modification de la conception ou du processus de fabrication. Bien que le PHPP ne soit pas exigé pour les pièces existantes, les sources du secteur estiment qu’il peut aider les entreprises de technologie médicale et de dispositifs médicaux à respecter les exigences réglementaires et, en général, à garantir la qualité, la sécurité et la conformité. Quels sont les avantages de l’utilisation du PHPP ? Essentiellement, le PHPP confirme qu’un processus de fabrication peut produire de manière cohérente et fiable une pièce de qualité. Mais c’est peut-être trop général. Le dernier mot revient à l’Automotive Industry Action Group, qui est à l’origine de cette norme de qualité. Ce groupe déclare que le PHPP : Fournit un processus d’homologation des pièces uniforme Garantit que les pièces répondent aux spécifications du client Fournit la preuve de la fiabilité du processus Contrôle le processus de modification des produits et des processus, en fournissant un point d’homologation pour toutes les modifications afin de garantir la conformité avec le niveau d’assemblage/processus suivant Options d’inspection supplémentaires En plus de notre processus standard, nous proposons diverses options de mesure de la qualité, d’inspection et de documentation, en collaborant avec vous pour nous assurer que nous respectons notre norme stricte de livraison de pièces moulées par injection de haute qualité. Outre le PHPP, d’autres options de rapports d’inspection incluent des méthodes de mesure telles que différents points de contrôle du premier article, le contrôle critique pour la qualité et les rapports d’inspection numériques, qui sont disponibles au moment de l’achat. Protolabs Network propose également le PHPP pour l’usinage CNC et d’autres gammes de services sur demande. title: SEO for Apps 2026: The Complete ASO Strategy Guide
summary: Got a new app you need to market on the Google Playstore or Apple Appstore? Here are our quick tips for doing SEO for apps along with ASO tools to use.
body_text: You’ve built a great app, but for some reason, people aren’t downloading it, or worse, they don’t even know it exists. That problem hasn’t changed since app stores existed. What has changed is almost everything about how to fix it. The App Store now holds around 2.19 million apps and Google Play has over 1.5 million , which means a good app no longer gets found on its own. Both platforms overhauled their ranking logic in 2025, shifting weight toward retention, engagement, and even the text inside your screenshots. This guide covers what has actually changed in terms of SEO for apps , what still matters, and how to build an ASO strategy that holds up under today’s algorithms. TL;DR ASO and organic acquisition are no longer separate from retention. Both Apple and Google now factor in how long users stick around after they install, not just how many people download. Screenshot text is now a ranking signal on iOS , following Apple’s 2025 algorithm update, which means your visual assets need to be treated as keyword-aware content, not just design. Keyword placement still matters, but character limits and platform rules differ significantly between the App Store and Google Play, and treating them the same is a common, costly mistake. Ratings and reviews function as a gatekeeper , not just a ranking input. Most users read at least one review before installing, and apps under a 4.0 rating rarely make it into featured placements. Localization is a ranking lever, not just a translation task , especially with over half the world’s mobile users based in Asia-Pacific and the majority not speaking English as a first language. AI is reshaping app discovery itself , with users increasingly researching apps through conversational AI assistants before ever opening a store, adding a new discovery layer ASO teams are still learning to influence. SEO for Apps vs. ASO, and Why You Need Both “SEO for apps” is usually one of the first searches a founder runs before launching a new app, but SEO and ASO solve two different problems that both matter for discoverability. SEO (Search Engine Optimization) governs whether your app, or the web content around it, shows up in a general search engine like Google or Bing. ASO (App Store Optimization) governs whether your app shows up and converts once someone is searching inside the App Store or Google Play. ASO is not a one-time setup. Store algorithms, competitor listings, and seasonal user behavior all shift constantly, so ranking maintenance has to be an ongoing effort, not a launch-week checklist. A meaningful share of app discovery still happens through mobile web search , not just in-store search, so skipping SEO because you have ASO covered leaves real visibility on the table. Treating these as the same discipline, or worse, ignoring one entirely, is one of the most common mistakes early-stage app teams make. What Changed in 2025 That Still Matters in 2026 The last two years reset several of the assumptions ASO strategies used to rely on. A few shifts in particular are still actively shaping rankings heading through 2026. Screenshot text became a ranking factor on iOS. Apple’s algorithm update began indexing the caption text layered over App Store screenshots, meaning your visuals now function as keyword-aware content rather than pure design. Custom Product Pages went organic. What used to be a paid-traffic-only tool can now appear in organic App Store search, and Apple has since doubled the number of Custom Product Pages developers can publish per app. Google shifted its algorithm from install volume toward retention. An app that gets downloaded a lot but loses users quickly no longer ranks as well as one with strong retention, even at a lower download volume. App stability and update frequency now visibly affect rankings. Crashes, slow load times, and stale apps are read as quality signals by both platforms, not just user experience issues. AI-generated app tags and semantic search are expanding. Apple’s App Store Tags use AI to label apps based on metadata, screenshots, and descriptions, which then influence which “similar apps” a user gets shown during browsing. Optimizing your app for search is wasted effort if the app itself isn’t stable, fast, and worth sticking around for. In 2026, the algorithms notice retention just as much as users do. Keyword Optimization: What Still Works, and What’s Changed Keyword research remains foundational to ASO, but the placement rules and the platforms’ tolerance for keyword stuffing have gotten stricter and more nuanced. Prioritize keywords with strong estimated traffic and manageable competition. These are still the fastest path to visibility, especially for a new app with no existing ranking history to lean on. Front-load descriptive keywords into your app title , since title placement carries more ranking weight than body copy, and it also tells a searching user immediately what your app does. Respect platform-specific character limits. Google Play allows a 50-character title with up to 4,000 characters of description. The App Store limits titles to 30 characters, but adds a 30-character subtitle field and a 100-character keyword field, none of which should repeat words already used elsewhere. Avoid keyword stuffing entirely. Both platforms now weigh natural language and readability more heavily, and a description packed with repeated exact-match keywords reads as spam to the algorithm and to the user. Don’t change your app title frequently just to chase a trending keyword. Frequent title changes can hurt both your brand recognition and your ranking stability, since algorithms tend to reward consistency over churn. Refresh your keyword set on a quarterly cadence at minimum. Search behavior, competitor positioning, and seasonal trends shift often enough that a keyword list from launch day is rarely still optimal a year later. Visual Assets Now Carry Ranking Weight, Not Just Conversion Weight Screenshots and preview videos used to be purely a conversion lever. That is no longer entirely true. Treat your first two to three screenshots as the entire pitch. Most users never scroll past them, so your core value proposition needs to land immediately, not build up gradually across a gallery. Write screenshot captions as keyword-aware copy , since Apple’s algorithm update now reads that text as part of your app’s indexed content, not just as design decoration. Keep text readable on the smallest supported screen size. If a caption is illegible on a compact device, you are losing conversions on every user viewing from that screen size. Invest in icon testing. Your icon is your most frequent brand impression across the store, and even a small lift in tap-through rate compounds meaningfully across total impressions. Add video where the platform supports it. Preview videos and promo videos are earning more ranking and conversion weight in 2026 as user attention spans continue shrinking. Ratings, Reviews, and Why They Function as a Gatekeeper Ratings and reviews are no longer just a trust signal buried at the bottom of your listing. They function closer to a gate that low performers simply cannot get past. Most users check reviews before installing. The overwhelming majority of users read at least one review before downloading a free app, and even more do so before a paid one. A rating below 4.0 quietly caps your visibility. Most apps that make it into featured placements sit at or above a 4.0 average, and algorithmic ranking treats rating as an indirect but meaningful signal. Respond to negative reviews quickly and specifically. A real, non-templated response within a day or two often prompts users to revise a negative rating once their issue is actually addressed. Reviews are fully indexed on Google Play. Keywords that show up naturally in user reviews create additional discovery paths for your app, which is not the case on iOS. App Localization Is a Ranking Strategy, Not a Translation Task There are close to 4.8 billion mobile users worldwide, and the majority of them do not use English as a primary or secondary language, with more than half concentrated in the Asia-Pacific region. An app without a real localization strategy is leaving most of the global market on the table. Localize metadata for each target store, not just the app’s interface. Keywords that convert well in English often do not translate directly, and the best-performing local keywords need their own research. Support the technical requirements of your target languages , including right-to-left scripts, vertical text, and non-Latin character input, wherever your target markets require them. Use native speakers for translation and proofreading, never automatic translation alone. A mistranslated phrase can shift meaning entirely, and the resulting bad review costs more than the translation would have. Remember that iOS and Google Play handle localization indexing differently. Apple allows cross-localization, where one storefront can index keywords from multiple languages, while Google Play indexes only the single locale you select, description included. Comparison: ASO Before vs. ASO in 2026 Factor The Old Approach What Works in 2026 Ranking signals Keywords and download volume Keywords, retention, engagement, and screenshot text Screenshots Purely visual, conversion-only Indexed content that also affects ranking on iOS Custom Product Pages Paid traffic only Appear in organic search results App stability Loosely connected to ranking A direct, visible ranking factor Localization Translation of existing copy Full metadata and keyword research per market Discovery path App store search only Store search plus AI assistant recommendations Where AI Is Starting to Change App Discovery A newer shift worth watching closely through the rest of 2026 is how conversational AI interfaces are entering the app discovery funnel before a user ever opens a store. People increasingly research app options through AI assistants first, then head to the App Store or Google Play already knowing roughly what they want. Semantic and intent-based matching is becoming more important than exact keyword matching alone , both inside app store search and in how AI assistants describe and recommend apps. Traditional ASO metadata may not always be the first touchpoint anymore , which means clarity and accuracy in how your app is described matters beyond just the store listing itself. This is an emerging area, not yet a fully mapped discipline. ASO teams are still learning how much influence they have over AI-assisted discovery, but the apps investing in clear, accurate, well-structured metadata now are better positioned as this channel matures. Getting the Foundation Right Before You Optimize None of this matters if the underlying app is not robust, scalable, or reliable. Ranking algorithms in 2026 actively penalize crashes, slow performance, and poor retention, which means ASO strategy and product quality are no longer separate conversations. Appscrip builds native, scalable apps across marketplaces, super apps, social platforms, and more , so the product behind your ASO strategy is stable enough for the algorithms, and the users, to reward it.
